# Learning to Reason in LLMs by Expectation Maximization

Junghyun Lee Affiliation: Kim Jaechul Graduate School of AI, KAIST,
Seoul, Republic of Korea Correspondence to: <jh_lee00@kaist.ac.kr>   
Branislav Kveton Affiliation: Adobe Research, San Jose, CA, USA    Anup
Rao Affiliation: Adobe Research, San Jose, CA, USA    Subhojyoti
Mukherjee Affiliation: Adobe Research, San Jose, CA, USA    Ryan A.
Rossi Affiliation: Adobe Research, San Jose, CA, USA    Sunav Choudhary
Affiliation: Adobe Research, San Jose, CA, USA    Alexa Siu
Affiliation: Adobe Research, San Jose, CA, USA

###### Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) solve reasoning problems by first
generating a rationale and then answering. We formalize reasoning as a
latent variable model and derive a reward-based filtered
expectation-maximization (FEM) objective for learning to reason. This
view connects EM and modern reward-based optimization, and shows that
the main challenge lies in designing a sampling distribution of
rationales that justify correct answers. We instantiate and compare
three sampling schemes: rejection sampling with a budget, self-taught
reasoner (STaR), and prompt posterior sampling (PPS), which only keeps
the rationalization stage of STaR that conditions on the correct answer
in the prompt. We experiment with LLM-as-a-judge calibration and
summarization from feedback tasks, where conditioning on the correct
answer provides a strong guidance for generating rationales. Our
experiments show the efficacy of PPS over other sampling schemes, and
that the sampling scheme can have a significant impact on performance.

## 1 Introduction

_Large language models (LLMs)_ have shown strong performance on
reasoning tasks, such as math word problems and multiple-choice
exams ([Zelikman et al., 2022](#bib.bib14); [Shao et al.,
2024](#bib.bib8)). In these tasks, it is often difficult to answer
questions directly. Instead, it is more beneficial to first generate an
intermediate _reasoning trace_ or _rationale_, and then output the
answer. This is the key idea in _chain-of-thought (CoT)_ prompting,
where the model is asked to _think step by step_ before answering ([Wei
et al., 2022](#bib.bib30); [Kojima et al., 2022](#bib.bib31)).

Reasoning as a latent variable model (LVM). We consider the task of
learning a mapping from a question $`x`$ to its answer $`y^{\star}`$,
and specifically focus on deterministically verifiable answers. This
setting is common in domains like math reasoning ([DeepSeek-AI,
2025](#bib.bib27)), multiple-choice question-answering ([Hendrycks et
al., 2021a](#bib.bib55)), and learning LLM judges or reward models from
human feedback ([Chiang et al., 2025](#bib.bib10); [Ankner et al.,
2024](#bib.bib9); [Sahoo et al., 2025](#bib.bib57)). When the task is
complex, it is hard to model $`x\rightarrow y^{\star}`$ directly. This
motivates the introduction of a rationale – a _latent variable_ $`z`$
representing the (unobserved) intermediate reasoning process. In words,
conditioned on both the question $`x`$ and rationale $`z`$, the model
has a much higher chance of generating the correct answer $`y^{\star}`$
than when conditioned on $`x`$ alone. With the rationale, the predictive
structure factors as a *latent variable model (LVM)* ([Koller and
Friedman, 2009](#bib.bib60)):

|     | This latent-variable perspective on rationales has been explored in
various forms in prior works ([Zelikman et al., 2022](#bib.bib14); [Yuan
et al., 2023](#bib.bib15); [Phan et al., 2023](#bib.bib19); [Hu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib21); [Zhong et al., 2025](#bib.bib23); [Tang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib24); [Xu, 2025](#bib.bib25)). We adopt it as a starting
point for understanding existing _learning to reason_ algorithms and, in
particular, the role of sampling.

Expectation maximization (EM). Once rationales are modeled as latent
variables, the *EM algorithm* ([Dempster et al., 1977](#bib.bib35);
[Moon, 1996](#bib.bib40); [Neal and Hinton, 1998](#bib.bib41)) can be
used to learn them. The algorithm alternates between computing a
posterior distribution over rationales conditioned on the observed
question-answer pairs (E-step) and maximizing the expected complete data
log-likelihood (M-step). Neither of the steps can be implemented exactly
in LLMs. The E-step requires computing an expectation over $`z`$
conditioned on both $`x`$ and $`y^{\star}`$ in
([1](#S1.E1 "Equation 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Learning to Reason in LLMs by Expectation Maximization")).
The expectation does not have a closed form, and approximating it via
Monte Carlo sampling requires sampling from the exact posterior. In
theory, classic statistical techniques, such as rejection
sampling ([Neal and Hinton, 1998](#bib.bib41)) and Markov chain Monte
Carlo ([Wei and Tanner, 1990](#bib.bib36); [Doucet et al.,
2001](#bib.bib1); [Phan et al., 2023](#bib.bib19)), could be used, but
they are not guaranteed to be computationally or statistically
inefficient. The M-step also lacks a closed-form solution and is
typically approximated by gradient-based optimization ([Bottou et al.,
2018](#bib.bib61)). Many prior works ([Balakrishnan et al.,
2017](#bib.bib42); [Neath, 2013](#bib.bib37); [Cappé and Moulines,
2009](#bib.bib2)) studied this and similar approaches.

Self-improvement in LLMs. Concurrently, the LLM community has introduced
algorithms that train LLMs by explicitly generating and filtering their
own reasoning traces, a paradigm known as _self-improvement_. Examples
include rejection-based fine-tuning ([Yuan et al., 2023](#bib.bib15);
[Dong et al., 2023](#bib.bib17); [Singh et al., 2024](#bib.bib20); [Shao
et al., 2024](#bib.bib8)) and self-taught reasoning ([Zelikman et al.,
2022](#bib.bib14)). These methods share a similar high-level structure:

1.  1.  Sample one or more rationale-answer pairs $`z,\hat{y}`$ conditioned
        on the question $`x`$;
2.  2.  Verify if $`\hat{y}=y^{\star}`$;
3.  3.  Fine-tune on accepted rationale-answer pairs.

From the LVM perspective, these methods perform approximate E-steps
followed by M-steps. While [Zelikman et al. (2022)](#bib.bib14) noted
this link, they focused on a policy-gradient justification for their
proposed self-taught reasoner, leaving the formal EM connection
under-explored.

Contributions. In this work, we examine this connection in detail. Our
contributions are as follows:

- •
  Formalizing reasoning as filtered EM. We revisit LLM reasoning as an
  LVM and derive a reward-based _filtered EM_
  ($`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt FEM`$) objective. We approximate the E-step
  via a single Monte Carlo sample and the M-step using a _filtered_
  gradient update. At a high level, we sample rationale-answer pairs
  from the latest model for all questions, keep them if the sampled
  answer is correct, and then fine-tune on the retained pairs. This
  formulation rigorously relates EM to modern reward-based optimization
  and frames LLM self-improvement as an iterative supervised fine-tuning
  procedure where latent rationales are resampled at each epoch. We also
  highlight its connection to reward-weighted fine-tuning of [Mukherjee
  et al. (2025)](#bib.bib34).
- •
  Unifying and instantiating sampling schemes. We demonstrate that
  existing _learning to reason_ algorithms, such as rejection sampling
  ($`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt RS`$) and self-taught reasoning
  ($`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt STaR`$), can be viewed as specific instances
  of our $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt FEM`$ framework with different
  rationale sampling schemes. Furthermore, we propose prompt posterior
  sampling ($`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPS`$), which can be viewed as the
  second rationalization stage of $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt STaR`$ and, to
  the best of our knowledge, has not yet been systematically studied.
- •
  Empirical evaluation of sampling schemes. We empirically evaluate all
  sampling schemes on LLM-as-a-judge calibration ([Zheng et al.,
  2023](#bib.bib7); [Sahoo et al., 2025](#bib.bib57)) and summarization
  from feedback ([Stiennon et al., 2020](#bib.bib54)) tasks. The
  evaluation is conducted on two Llama ([Llama Team, 2024](#bib.bib50))
  and three Qwen ([Qwen Team, 2024](#bib.bib51)) models. Unlike in
  complex math reasoning ([Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib8)), conditioning
  on the correct answer provides a strong guiding signal for rationale
  generation in our tasks, and this is why we experiment with them. We
  observe that $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPS`$ consistently outperforms
  other sampling schemes. Our results show that the _sampling scheme_
  approximating the E-step is critical to the effectiveness of
  self-improvement in LLMs.

## 2 EM and Learning to Reason

Algorithm 1 Filtered EM ($`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt FEM`$) for learning to
reason.

Let $`{\mathcal{D}}=\{(x_{i},y_{i}^{\star})\}_{i=1}^{N}`$ be a dataset
of $`N`$ question-answer pairs. We denote the probability that an LLM
$`\pi(\cdot\mid\cdot;\theta)`$ with parameters $`\theta`$ generates an
answer $`y`$ when prompted with $`x`$ by $`\pi(y\mid x;\theta)`$. For
reasoning models that generate rationales, we write
$`\pi(z,y\mid x;\theta)`$ for the joint probability distribution over a
rationale $`z`$ and final answer $`y`$. We denote by $`\nabla`$ the
gradient operator with respect to $`\theta`$.

As discussed in detail in
[Section 1](#S1 "1 Introduction ‣ Learning to Reason in LLMs by Expectation Maximization"),
we model reasoning using a latent variable $`z_{i}`$ because learning
$`x_{i}\rightarrow z_{i},y_{i}^{\star}`$ leads to more accurate answers
than $`x_{i}\rightarrow y_{i}^{\star}`$ alone. Intuitively, $`z_{i}`$ is
the underlying reasoning, and therefore, conditioned on both $`x_{i}`$
and $`z_{i}`$, the LLM is more likely to generate correct answers
$`y_{i}^{\star}`$. A standard way of learning LVMs is the *EM
algorithm* ([Dempster et al., 1977](#bib.bib35)). EM is an iterative
algorithm with two steps in each iteration. The E-step computes the
expected complete data log-likelihood given the most recent model
parameter $`\theta^{(k-1)}`$,

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\textstyle{\mathcal{J}}(\theta):=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{E}_{z_{i}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x_{i},y_{i}^{\star};\theta^{(k-1)})}[\log\pi(z_{i},y_{i}^{\star}\mid x_{i};\theta)]\,,
``` |  |

where $`\pi(\cdot\mid x_{i},y_{i}^{\star};\theta^{(k-1)})`$ is the
posterior distribution of the latent rationale $`z_{i}`$ under the
previous iterate $`\theta^{(k-1)}`$. The M-step solves for
$`\theta^{(k)}=\argmax_{\theta}{\mathcal{J}}(\theta)`$.

### 2.1 From EM to Reward-Weighted Fine-Tuning

We first focus on the M-step and introduce a series of approximations
that lead our algorithm. First, we approximate the exact maximization by
a single step of gradient ascent

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\theta^{(k)}\leftarrow\theta^{(k)}+\eta^{(k)}\underbrace{\nabla\,\mathbb{E}_{\hat{z}_{i}}[\log\pi(\hat{z}_{i},y_{i}^{\star}\mid x_{i};\theta)]}_{(*)}
``` |  | (2) |

for each data point $`i\in[N]`$, where $`\eta^{(k)}`$ is the learning
rate at iteration $`k`$ and the expectation $`\mathbb{E}_{\hat{z}_{i}}`$
is taken with respect to
$`\hat{z}_{i}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x_{i},y_{i}^{\star};\theta^{(k-1)})`$.

Now note that the posterior distribution is by definition *consistent*
with the evidence that we condition on. Therefore, any
$`\hat{z}_{i},\hat{y}_{i}`$ drawn from
$`\pi(\cdot\mid x_{i},y_{i}^{\star})`$ must satisfy
$`\hat{y}_{i}=y_{i}^{\star}`$ almost surely. This implies that checking
whether the generated answer matches the ground truth is theoretically
equivalent to enforcing the posterior distribution’s support. Thus, even
if one were to sample from a broader proposal distribution, applying a
consistency filter ensures that the update operates only on
answer-consistent samples. We formalize this using a binary reward
$`r(\hat{y}_{i},y_{i}^{\star}):=\mathds{1}[\hat{y}_{i}=y_{i}^{\star}]`$,
which lets us rewrite
([2](#S2.E2 "Equation 2 ‣ 2.1 From EM to Reward-Weighted Fine-Tuning ‣ 2 EM and Learning to Reason ‣ Learning to Reason in LLMs by Expectation Maximization"))
with

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
(*)=\nabla\,\mathbb{E}_{\hat{z}_{i},\hat{y}_{i}}[r(\hat{y}_{i},y_{i}^{\star})\log\pi(\hat{z}_{i},\hat{y}_{i}\mid x_{i};\theta)]\,,
``` |  | (3) |

where the expectation $`\mathbb{E}_{\hat{z}_{i},\hat{y}_{i}}`$ is taken
with respect to
$`\hat{z}_{i},\hat{y}_{i}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x_{i},y_{i}^{\star};\theta^{(k-1)})`$.

We make two additional observations. First, the expectation is defined
with respect to a distribution that depends only on the previous
parameters $`\theta^{(k-1)}`$, but not the optimized $`\theta`$. Second,
the reward does not depend on $`\theta`$. As a result, the gradient can
be moved inside the expectation and we get

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
(*)=\mathbb{E}_{\hat{z}_{i},\hat{y}_{i}}[r(\hat{y}_{i},y_{i}^{\star})\nabla\log\pi(\hat{z}_{i},\hat{y}_{i}\mid x_{i};\theta)]\,.
``` |  | (4) |

In LLMs, this expectation cannot be computed efficiently because
$`\hat{z}_{i},\hat{y}_{i}`$ are sequences of tokens from an
exponentially large space. Therefore, we approximate it by a single
Monte Carlo sample as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
(*)\approx r(\hat{y}_{i},y_{i}^{\star})\nabla\log\pi(\hat{z}_{i},\hat{y}_{i}\mid x_{i};\theta)\,,
``` |  | (5) |

where
$`\hat{z}_{i},\hat{y}_{i}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x_{i},y_{i}^{\star};\theta^{(k-1)})`$
is a single rationale-answer sample. This is a *filtered* gradient
update of the classic Monte-Carlo EM ([Wei and Tanner,
1990](#bib.bib36); [Neath, 2013](#bib.bib37)), where the reward
$`r(\hat{y}_{i},y_{i}^{\star})`$ serves as a filter in broader proposal
distributions
([Section 3](#S3 "3 Rationale Sampling ‣ Learning to Reason in LLMs by Expectation Maximization")).

Input: Data point $`(x,y^{\star})`$ , budget
$`M\in{\mathbb{N}}`$$`m=1,\dots,M`$$`\hat{z}_{m},\hat{y}_{m}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x;\theta)`$$`\hat{y}_{m}=y^{\star}`$Output:$`\hat{z}_{m},y^{\star}`$Output:$`\hat{z}_{M},\hat{y}_{M}`$

\For\State\If\State\EndIf\EndFor\State

### 2.2 Practical Meta-Algorithm

Exact sampling of $`\hat{z}_{i},\hat{y}_{i}`$ from the posterior
distribution in
([5](#S2.E5 "Equation 5 ‣ 2.1 From EM to Reward-Weighted Fine-Tuning ‣ 2 EM and Learning to Reason ‣ Learning to Reason in LLMs by Expectation Maximization"))
is computationally infeasible in LLMs. This is because sampling from the
posterior requires inverting the generative process in
([1](#S1.E1 "Equation 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Learning to Reason in LLMs by Expectation Maximization"))
to obtain reasoning paths $`\hat{z}_{i}`$ leading to correct answers
$`y_{i}^{\star}`$. Moreover, $`\hat{z}_{i},\hat{y}_{i}`$ are sequences
of tokens from an exponentially large space.

We address this challenge by considering a generic *rationale proposal
distribution* $`q(\hat{z},\hat{y}\mid x,y^{\star};\theta)`$ and
implement it by *prompting* the most recent model $`\theta^{(k-1)}`$.
Then we approximate
([5](#S2.E5 "Equation 5 ‣ 2.1 From EM to Reward-Weighted Fine-Tuning ‣ 2 EM and Learning to Reason ‣ Learning to Reason in LLMs by Expectation Maximization"))
by sampling
$`\hat{z}_{i},\hat{y}_{i}\sim q(\cdot\mid x_{i},y_{i}^{\star};\theta^{(k-1)})`$.
More specifically, for each data point, we sample
$`\hat{z}_{i},\hat{y}_{i}`$; keep it only if the sampled answer is
correct, $`\hat{y}_{i}=y_{i}^{\star}`$; and then fine-tune on retained
$`\hat{z}_{i},\hat{y}_{i}`$. Because the reward
$`r(\hat{y}_{i},y_{i}^{\star})`$ is binary, the rationales leading to
incorrect answers are filtered out in the gradient update.

The pseudo-code of our algorithm is given in
[Algorithm 1](#alg1 "In 2 EM and Learning to Reason ‣ Learning to Reason in LLMs by Expectation Maximization").
We call it *filtered EM ($`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt FEM`$)* due to reward
filtering in
([5](#S2.E5 "Equation 5 ‣ 2.1 From EM to Reward-Weighted Fine-Tuning ‣ 2 EM and Learning to Reason ‣ Learning to Reason in LLMs by Expectation Maximization")).
The algorithm is iterative. In each iteration, it applies the E- and
M-steps
([Section 2.1](#S2.SS1 "2.1 From EM to Reward-Weighted Fine-Tuning ‣ 2 EM and Learning to Reason ‣ Learning to Reason in LLMs by Expectation Maximization"))
to all question-answer pairs sequentially: Line 3 is the E-step applied
to dataset $`{\mathcal{D}}`$ and Line 5 is the corresponding M-step with
reward filtering. For simplicity of exposition, we assume a batch size
of $`1`$. The design of $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt FEM`$ is motivated by
*supervised fine-tuning (SFT)*. In particular, each iteration of
$`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt FEM`$ can be viewed as an epoch in SFT, where
the training data are adapted to the learned model due to sampling
$`\hat{z}_{i}^{(k)},\hat{y}_{i}^{(k)}`$ in Line 3. It can also be viewed
as reward-weighted fine-tuning ([Mukherjee et al., 2025](#bib.bib34)),
where the model is updated to increase the reward-weighted
log-likelihood of the sampled rationale-answer pairs.

The rationale proposal distribution $`q(\cdot\mid x,y^{\star};\theta)`$
is a design decision and should have two properties. First, the
probability of event $`\hat{y}=y^{\star}`$ should be maximized to
maximize the amount of training data. Second, the quality of rationales
$`\hat{z}`$ should be high to ensure that conditioning on $`x,\hat{z}`$
leads to better predicted answers $`\hat{y}`$ and generalization. We
provide different instantiations of $`q`$ in
[Section 3](#S3 "3 Rationale Sampling ‣ Learning to Reason in LLMs by Expectation Maximization").

### 2.3 Filtered EM and Reinforcement Learning

The filtered EM update can also be justified through its relationship to
reward-based maximization in *reinforcement learning (RL)*. To show
this, we build on the work of [Mukherjee et al. (2025)](#bib.bib34),
which extends results of [Ma et al. (2019)](#bib.bib4); [Liang and
Vlassis (2022)](#bib.bib16) from offline logged bandits to offline RL.

###### Lemma 1.

Let $`x,y^{\star}`$ be a question-answer pair and
$`r(\hat{y},y^{\star})=\mathds{1}[\hat{y}=y^{\star}]`$. Then for any
parameter vector $`\theta`$ and iteration $`k\geq 1`$,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{\hat{z},\hat{y}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x;\theta)}\!\left[r(\hat{y},y^{\star})\right]}_{\text{RHS}}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\geq\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{\hat{z},\hat{y}\sim q(\cdot\mid x,y^{\star};\theta^{(k-1)})}\!\left[r(\hat{y},y^{\star})\log\pi(\hat{z},\hat{y}\mid x;\theta)\right]}_{\text{LHS}}{}+C\,.`$ |  |

where $`C\geq 0`$ is independent of $`\theta`$. The inequality is tight
when
$`q(\cdot\mid x,y^{\star};\theta^{(k-1)})\equiv\pi(\cdot\mid x;\theta)`$.

###### Proof.

The proof mimics [Mukherjee et al. (2025)](#bib.bib34) and is provided
in
[Appendix A](#A1 "Appendix A Proof of ‣ Learning to Reason in LLMs by Expectation Maximization")
for completeness. ∎

The above lemma says that reward-weighted fine-tuning (LHS) essentially
optimizes a lower bound on the reward maximization objective (RHS). Our
$`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt FEM`$ update in
([5](#S2.E5 "Equation 5 ‣ 2.1 From EM to Reward-Weighted Fine-Tuning ‣ 2 EM and Learning to Reason ‣ Learning to Reason in LLMs by Expectation Maximization"))
iteratively refines it by alternating between updating the data sampling
distribution $`q`$ (E-step) and maximizing the lower bound (M-step).

## 3 Rationale Sampling

Now we instantiate the rationale proposal distribution
$`q(\cdot\mid x,y^{\star};\theta)`$ in
[Algorithm 1](#alg1 "In 2 EM and Learning to Reason ‣ Learning to Reason in LLMs by Expectation Maximization").
We focus on three representative schemes: rejection sampling with a
budget, self-taught reasoning, and prompt posterior sampling.

Rejection sampling with budget $`M`$ ($`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt RS`$). A
statistically correct way of sampling $`z`$ from the LVM in
([1](#S1.E1 "Equation 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Learning to Reason in LLMs by Expectation Maximization"))
is rejection sampling ([Neal and Hinton, 1998](#bib.bib41)). In LLMs, it
corresponds to sampling reasoning-answer pairs conditioned on the
question until the correct answer is sampled, with a budget of at most
$`M`$. The underlying intuition is to create a virtuous cycle: as the
model improves, it is more likely to sample correct answers, thereby
providing more training data for the next M-step. This approach has been
proposed before under the names of rejection fine-tuning ([Yuan et al.,
2023](#bib.bib15); [Dong et al., 2023](#bib.bib17); [Singh et al.,
2024](#bib.bib20)) and online rejection sampling fine-tuning ([Shao et
al., 2024](#bib.bib8), Appendix A.1.3). The pseudo-code of this method
is given in
[Algorithm 2](#alg2 "In 2.1 From EM to Reward-Weighted Fine-Tuning ‣ 2 EM and Learning to Reason ‣ Learning to Reason in LLMs by Expectation Maximization").

Prompt posterior sampling ($`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPS`$). Modern LLMs
are instruction fine-tuned to follow human feedback ([Ouyang et al.,
2022](#bib.bib6)). Therefore, one natural way of implementing posterior
sampling is by conditioning on the correct answer in the prompt, which
we show in
[Figure 1](#S3.F1 "In 3 Rationale Sampling ‣ Learning to Reason in LLMs by Expectation Maximization").
This directly addresses the computational inefficiency of
$`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt RS`$. Specifically, because the correct answer
is conditioned on, the model is likely to generate it and in this way
increase the fraction of accepted rationale-answer pairs. We note that
this does not *guarantee* that the model outputs the correct answer.
This also introduces a mismatch between training and testing. At
training time, the LLM generates rationales by conditioning on both the
question and answer, while at test time only the question is conditioned
on. We denote the corresponding sampling distribution by
$`q_{\textsc{pps}}(\cdot\mid x,y^{\star};\theta)`$. As we show below,
$`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPS`$ is essentially the second stage of
$`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt STaR`$.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 1: Our prompt and its posterior sampling variant. We set {task}
to the evaluated task, {response} to its solution, {judged score} to the
name of the metric, and {score rubrics} to its score rubrics. In prompt
posterior sampling, we add the cyan text and set {conditioning} to the

Self-taught reasoner sampling ($`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt STaR`$).
Introduced by the seminal work of [Zelikman et al. (2022)](#bib.bib14),
$`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt STaR`$ has the following two stages:

1.  1.
    A single rejection sampling step ($`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt RS`$ for
    $`M=1`$).
2.  2.
    If the sampled answer is not correct, $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt STaR`$
    samples a rationale-answer pair using a rationalization prompt, with
    the correct answer as a hint. This is precisely our proposed
    $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPS`$.

The pseudo-code of $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt STaR`$ is given in
[Algorithm 3](#alg3 "In 2.1 From EM to Reward-Weighted Fine-Tuning ‣ 2 EM and Learning to Reason ‣ Learning to Reason in LLMs by Expectation Maximization").
Conceptually, $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt STaR`$ chains
$`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt RS`$ and $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPS`$,
effectively sampling rationales from a mixture of the two distributions.
While this results in more accepted rationale-answer pairs on average
per $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt FEM`$ iteration than
$`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt RS`$ ($`M=1`$) and
$`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPS`$, we show empirically that the increased
quantity does not necessarily translate into quality. Instead, we
demonstrate that the *quality* of the sampling distribution $`q`$ is the
decisive factor.

## 4 Experiments

We evaluate $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt FEM`$ on *LLM-as-a-judge
calibration* ([Zheng et al., 2023](#bib.bib7); [Sahoo et al.,
2025](#bib.bib57)) and *summarization from feedback* ([Stiennon et al.,
2020](#bib.bib54)) tasks. We focus on these domains to highlight the
impact of sampling distributions, which has been overlooked due to the
community’s major focus on math reasoning ([Cobbe et al.,
2021](#bib.bib45); [Hendrycks et al., 2021b](#bib.bib56); [Shao et al.,
2024](#bib.bib8); [Lewkowycz et al., 2022](#bib.bib46); [Lightman et
al., 2024](#bib.bib47); [Trinh et al., 2024](#bib.bib48); [Luo et al.,
2025](#bib.bib49)). In complex math reasoning, conditioning on the final
answer is not expected to provide much benefit because the tasks are
complex. Our domains have unique properties that make them ideal for
investigating rationale sampling schemes:

1.  1.
    High information gain from $`y^{\star}`$. The correct answer is a
    human preference score. The score is readily available in public
    datasets, and conditioning on it significantly improves the
    generated rationale.
2.  2.
    Weak pre-trained models. Pre-trained base models tend to perform
    poorly on our tasks because they lack knowledge about human scores
    in the domain, even if they are given the same score rubric as
    humans.

### 4.1 Setting

We experiment with two Llama ([Llama Team, 2024](#bib.bib50)) (3B and
8B) and three Qwen ([Qwen Team, 2024](#bib.bib51)) (1.5B, 3B, and 7B)
models on two tasks.¹¹ 1 The specific models are Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct,
Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, and
Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct from HuggingeFace. The first task is calibration of
an LLM judge against human scores. We experiment with *HelpSteer2*
dataset ([Wang et al., 2024](#bib.bib52); [Wang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib53)), a collection of instruction-response pairs rated on
a $`5`$-point Likert scale. The quality of the responses is measured by
$`5`$ metrics: helpfulness, correctness, coherence, complexity, and
verbosity. The second task is predicting human quality scores for post
summaries. We experiment with *Summarize from Feedback* dataset ([Völske
et al., 2017](#bib.bib68); [Stiennon et al., 2020](#bib.bib54)), a
collection of Reddit post-summary pairs rated on a $`7`$-point Likert
scale. We use its axis subset, which contains $`4`$ metrics:
helpfulness, accuracy, coverage, and coherence. In summary, we evaluate
$`5`$ models on predicting $`9`$ metrics in two tasks. Our main prompt
is in
[Figure 1](#S3.F1 "In 3 Rationale Sampling ‣ Learning to Reason in LLMs by Expectation Maximization").
The system prompt and score rubrics are presented in
[Appendix B](#A2 "Appendix B Prompts ‣ Learning to Reason in LLMs by Expectation Maximization").

We evaluate three $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt FEM`$ sampling schemes:
$`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt RS`$ with budget $`M=1`$,
$`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt STaR`$, and $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPS`$; and
compare them to pre-trained base models and GPT-5.2. The E-step in (Line
3 in $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt FEM`$) is implemented using vLLM ([Kwon et
al., 2023](#bib.bib58)) and the M-step (Line 5 in
$`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt FEM`$) is implemented by SFT in TRL ([von Werra
et al., 2020](#bib.bib11)). We use AdamW ([Loshchilov and Hutter,
2019](#bib.bib59)) with default parameters and one epoch in SFT.
$`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt FEM`$ is run for $`K=5`$ iterations. The
learning rate decays linearly from $`\eta=10^{-6}`$ to $`\eta=10^{-7}`$
across the iterations, and it is kept constant within each iteration.
All experiments are conducted on NVIDIA A100 GPUs with resources scaled
by model size: 1B models on 1 GPU, 3B on 2 GPUs, and 7-8B on 4 GPUs. All
results are averaged over $`3`$ random runs with seeds $`257`$, $`521`$,
and $`1031`$. We sample a random subset of $`4\,000`$ data points
($`2\,000`$ train and $`2\,000`$ test) in each run. The sizes are chosen
so that the initialization overhead of vLLM and SFT is negligible in the
total runtime (less than $`20\%`$). Each run takes approximately $`60`$
minutes.

We report three metrics: test accuracy, data utilization, and reasoning
length in words. The test accuracy is the accuracy in predicting human
evaluation scores on a held-out test set, which we expect to improve as
the number of $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt FEM`$ iterations increases. The
data utilization is the percentage of accepted rationale-answer pairs,
which are used for training. We report this number to show that more
successful learning is not necessarily due to more training data. The
reasoning length shows whether the improved performance is due to deeper
or more compact reasoning.

Our results for Qwen 3B and HelpSteer2 correctness are reported in
[Figure 2](#S4.F2 "In 4 Experiments ‣ Learning to Reason in LLMs by Expectation Maximization").
The plots for all other models and metrics are reported in
[Appendix D](#A4 "Appendix D Detailed 𝙵𝙴𝙼 Runs ‣ Learning to Reason in LLMs by Expectation Maximization").
We observe two key trends. First, the test accuracies of
$`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt STaR`$ and $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPS`$
increase with more iterations and plateau, confirming the effectiveness
of multiple $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt FEM`$ iterations. Second,
$`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPS`$ outperforms all baselines across all
$`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt FEM`$ iterations, which we attribute to
generating superior rationales.

Crucially, the data utilization shows that this performance gain is not
driven by data quantity; $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPS`$ achieves a higher
accuracy with less training data than $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt STaR`$.
Instead, it is driven by the quality of reasoning. The reasoning length
of $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPS`$ increases to $`130`$ words versus less
than $`120`$ for $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt STaR`$. Qualitatively, the
longer reasoning is more comprehensive, and we illustrate it in
[Figure 3](#S4.F3 "In 4 Experiments ‣ Learning to Reason in LLMs by Expectation Maximization").
The final rationale resolves confusion in the original rationale, which
says that Jay and John cannot be brothers because they have the same
father. This mirrors observations in RL-based training ([DeepSeek-AI,
2025](#bib.bib27)) where models learn to reason more deeply.

We want to stress that this observed trend is model- and
domain-dependent, as can be seen in
[Appendix D](#A4 "Appendix D Detailed 𝙵𝙴𝙼 Runs ‣ Learning to Reason in LLMs by Expectation Maximization").
In some cases, the reasoning length *decreases* while accuracy improves.
This suggests that $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt FEM`$ does not blindly
encourage reasoning length, but rather learns to reason in a way that is
most suitable for the specific task and model: deeper reasoning for
complex judgments, or improving conciseness and compactness of the
language.

We summarize the highest accuracies attained by all sampling schemes in
[Tables 2](#S4.T2 "In 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Learning to Reason in LLMs by Expectation Maximization")
and [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Learning to Reason in LLMs by Expectation Maximization").
In HelpSteer2 experiments
([Table 2](#S4.T2 "In 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Learning to Reason in LLMs by Expectation Maximization")),
$`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPS`$ has the highest accuracy in $`22`$ out of
$`25`$ and $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt STaR`$ in $`3`$. Under the null
hypothesis that $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPS`$ and
$`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt STaR`$ perform identically, the p-value of
winning at least $`22`$ times is less than $`0.01`$. In Summarize from
Feedback experiments
([Table 2](#S4.T2 "In 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Learning to Reason in LLMs by Expectation Maximization")),
$`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPS`$ has the highest accuracy in $`15`$ out of
$`20`$, $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt STaR`$ in $`4`$, and they tie in one.
Under the null hypothesis that $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPS`$ and
$`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt STaR`$ perform identically, the p-value of
winning at least $`15`$ times is about $`0.02`$. We conclude that
$`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPS`$ outperforms the closest baseline with a
high statistical significance.

To further show that our tasks are non-trivial for state-of-the-art
LLMs, we evaluate GPT-5.2 as a strong baseline. In HelpSteer2 dataset,
GPT-5.2 achieves accuracies $`32.91\%`$ (helpfulness), $`30.84\%`$
(correctness), $`65.08\%`$ (coherence), $`58.88\%`$ (complexity), and
$`43.19\%`$ (verbosity). Our best fine-tuned models surpass these
numbers in all metrics but complexity. In Summarize from Feedback
dataset, GPT-5.2 achieves $`12.40\%`$ (helpfulness), $`69.91\%`$
(accuracy), $`16.40\%`$ (coverage), and $`50.43\%`$ (coherence).
Notably, our best fine-tuned models surpass all of these. This confirms
that our tasks genuinely benefit from adaptation to the domain.

### 4.3 Ablation Studies

We investigate the robustness of our findings through three ablation
studies with Qwen 3B
([Appendix C](#A3 "Appendix C Ablations Studies ‣ Learning to Reason in LLMs by Expectation Maximization")).
First, we vary the rejection sampling budget $`M\in\{1,3,5\}`$ in
$`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt RS`$. While increasing $`M`$ sometimes improves
performance through increased data utilization, it also increases
computation time linearly in $`M`$, and still significantly
underperforms $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPS`$ and
$`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt STaR`$. Second, we test the sensitivity of our
results to the prompt in
[Figure 1](#S3.F1 "In 3 Rationale Sampling ‣ Learning to Reason in LLMs by Expectation Maximization")
by conditioning less explicitly. We observe that less precise
conditioning decreases absolute performance of all sampling schemes.
However, the relative order remains the same, and
$`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPS`$ continues to outperform all baselines.
This shows that our results generalize beyond a single prompt and
highlights the importance of precise instructions when conditioning.
Finally, we also experiment with smaller and larger training set sizes.

## 5 Related Work

Our filtered EM ($`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt FEM`$) framework unifies
several recent approaches to self-improvement and reasoning under the
lens of inference. In this section, we explicate the connections to
specific EM-style algorithms, data filtering strategies, and the broader
RL as inference literature.

LLM self-improvement. $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt FEM`$ encompasses several
recent self-improvement algorithms for LLM reasoning. Notably,
ReSTEM ([Singh et al., 2024](#bib.bib20)) correspond to instantiating
the rationale proposal distribution $`q`$ in
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 2 EM and Learning to Reason ‣ Learning to Reason in LLMs by Expectation Maximization")
with standard *rejection sampling* ([Neal and Hinton,
1998](#bib.bib41)). This relationship arises from a specific modeling
choice: following the variational perspective of [Dayan and Hinton
(1997)](#bib.bib38), [Singh et al. (2024)](#bib.bib20) introduce a
binary optimality variable $`\mathcal{O}`$ and maximize
$`{\mathbb{P}}(\mathcal{O}=1\mid x)`$, treating the entire
trajectory—rationale $`z`$ and answer $`y`$—as a latent variable.
Consequently, their E-step filters samples from a fixed distribution:
the LLM conditioned *only* on the question $`x`$. Such reliance on a
fixed sampling distribution persists in recent literature as well. For
instance, LaTRO ([Chen et al., 2024](#bib.bib29)) introduces a
variational framework optimizing a lower bound on correct answer
likelihood; [Xu (2025)](#bib.bib25) proposes EM Policy Gradient to
stabilize off-policy updates; and RAFT++ ([Xiong et al.,
2025](#bib.bib18)) proposes a filtered version of PPO ([Schulman et al.,
2017](#bib.bib26)). In all these cases, the algorithms operate under a
fixed sampling policy $`\pi(z,y\mid x;\theta)`$ that conditions only on
the question.

Other works have explored alternative proposal distributions, but
typically through complex probabilistic machinery or separate inference
networks. TRICE ([Phan et al., 2023](#bib.bib19)) addresses the high
variance of gradient estimators in the M-step using control variates.
BRiTE ([Zhong et al., 2025](#bib.bib23)) targets the E-step by jointly
training a separate LLM to approximate the posterior via reinforcement
learning. Similarly, [Hu et al. (2024)](#bib.bib21) propose amortizing
intractable posterior inference using GFlowNets ([Bengio et al.,
2023](#bib.bib22)); although they do not apply this to iterative LLM
training, it shares the limitation of requiring a separate trained
network to sample from the true posterior.

Our $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt FEM`$ explores a more lightweight
alternative: leveraging the LLM’s inherent reasoning and
instruction-following capabilities ([Bai et al., 2022](#bib.bib32);
[Ouyang et al., 2022](#bib.bib6); [Wei et al., 2022](#bib.bib30);
[Kojima et al., 2022](#bib.bib31)) to approximate $`q`$ via prompting,
thereby avoiding the complexity of training auxiliary models. We
demonstrate that in notable domains, such as calibrating LLM-as-a-judge,
this EM-based approach can be vastly improved by simply changing the
sampling distribution to that of rationales conditioned on the true
answer. This highlights that, as prior work has overlooked, examining
the sampling scheme offers a simple yet effective direction to further
improve the training efficiency of LLM reasoning.

Filtering and implicit objectives. Beyond iterative algorithms, our work
connects to the literature, viewing data filtration as implicit
objective modification. [Shrivastava et al. (2025)](#bib.bib28) propose
oversampling reasoning traces and applying top-$`K`$ filtering, arguing
that such filtration acts as a form of reward shaping. Similarly, [Karan
and Du (2025)](#bib.bib33) shows that inference-time sampling from a
sharpened distribution can outperform RL-based post-training. From a
distributional perspective, methods like Quark ([Khalifa et al.,
2021](#bib.bib63)) and others ([Go et al., 2023](#bib.bib62);
[Kruszewski et al., 2025](#bib.bib65); [Kim et al., 2025](#bib.bib64))
derive objectives by defining a target distribution that discards
incorrect answers while preserving the relative probabilities of correct
ones, often approximated via information projection ([Amari,
1985](#bib.bib66); [Nielsen, 2018](#bib.bib67)).

Our work is complementary to this line of research: we adopt a
latent-variable perspective, treating such filtering as an implicit
target distribution over rationales and answers, and study how different
choices of the *sampling* distribution in the E-step affect learning via
our $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt FEM`$. Rather than viewing filtering as a
heuristic for dataset cleaning, $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt FEM`$ frames it
as a formal approximation of the posterior in a latent variable model.

RL as probabilistic inference. Finally, the derivation of
$`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt FEM`$ is grounded in the probabilistic
formulation of RL, also known as Control as Inference; see our
discussions with
Lemma [1](#Thmlemma1 "Lemma 1. ‣ 2.3 Filtered EM and Reinforcement Learning ‣ 2 EM and Learning to Reason ‣ Learning to Reason in LLMs by Expectation Maximization").
The paradigm of addressing RL problems via Expectation-Maximization is
well established in control theory ([Dayan and Hinton,
1997](#bib.bib38); [Levine, 2018](#bib.bib44)), having been investigated
through various lenses, including mixture models ([Vlassis and
Toussaint, 2009](#bib.bib43)) and MCMC approximations ([Hoffman et al.,
2007](#bib.bib39)). While this theoretical equivalence is
well-documented in general RL, our work systematically operationalizes
it for LLM reasoning. We underscore that, in the context of LLMs, the
choice of sampling distribution is not merely a heuristic choice but a
central component of the variational objective.

## 6 Conclusions

We revisit reasoning as a latent-variable model, bridging the gap
between learning to reason, filtered EM, and reward-based policy
gradients. Our work highlights the critical role of rationale sampling
distributions, a factor that may have a major impact on empirical
performance. In the process, we propose prompt posterior sampling, a
simple yet effective sampling scheme corresponding to the
rationalization stage of $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt STaR`$. In our
experiments, prompt posterior sampling consistently outperforms other
sampling schemes, including rejection sampling and
$`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt STaR`$, on two human-rating alignment tasks in
HelpSteer2 and Summarize from Feedback datasets.

Limitations. First, we establish that the sampling distribution is an
important domain-specific hyperparameter. Our results on alignment tasks
provide a definitive proof of concept: the “right” choice of the
rationale sampling distribution in $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt FEM`$ leads
to substantial empirical gains. In future work, we plan to experiment
with more complex tasks, such as math reasoning, and to explore richer
guiding signals. Second, our current algorithm design is motivated by
SFT, in which each iteration is essentially a single epoch during which
the training data are adapted to the learned model using sampled
rationales. In future work, we plan to investigate if our improvements
in sampling generalize to online reinforcement learning, such as GRPO
([Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib8)). When viewed in this way, our current
design is reminiscent of batch RL ([Lange et al., 2012](#bib.bib3);
[Jaques et al., 2020](#bib.bib5); [Levine, 2018](#bib.bib44)), also with
connections to prior literature on expert iterations ([Anthony et al.,
2017](#bib.bib12); [Anthony, 2021](#bib.bib13)) Last but not least,
while all of our approximations in
[Section 2.1](#S2.SS1 "2.1 From EM to Reward-Weighted Fine-Tuning ‣ 2 EM and Learning to Reason ‣ Learning to Reason in LLMs by Expectation Maximization")
are properly justified, we have not formally analyzed
$`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt FEM`$, which we also leave for future work. This
is because we focused on developing the algorithmic framework and
empirically validating it.

## Impact Statement

This paper presents work whose goal is to advance the field of machine
learning. There are many potential societal consequences of our work,
none of which we feel must be specifically highlighted here.

## Appendix A Proof of [Lemma 1](#Thmlemma1 "Lemma 1. ‣ 2.3 Filtered EM and Reinforcement Learning ‣ 2 EM and Learning to Reason ‣ Learning to Reason in LLMs by Expectation Maximization")

The lemma follows from simple algebraic manipulations,

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\hat{z},\hat{y}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x;\theta)}\!\left[r(\hat{y},y^{\star})\right]={}`$ | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\hat{z},\hat{y}\sim q(\cdot\mid x,y^{\star};\theta^{(k-1)})}\!\left[r(\hat{y},y^{\star})\frac{\pi(\hat{z},\hat{y}\mid x;\theta)}{q(\hat{z},\hat{y}\mid x,y^{\star};\theta^{(k-1)})}\right]`$ |  |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle\geq{}`$ | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\hat{z},\hat{y}\sim q(\cdot\mid x,y^{\star};\theta^{(k-1)})}\!\left[r(\hat{y},y^{\star})\left(1+\log\frac{\pi(\hat{z},\hat{y}\mid x;\theta)}{q(\hat{z},\hat{y}\mid x,y^{\star};\theta^{(k-1)})}\right)\right]`$ |  | ($`z\geq 1+\log z`$) |
|  | $`\displaystyle={}`$ | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\hat{z},\hat{y}\sim q(\cdot\mid x,y^{\star};\theta^{(k-1)})}\!\left[r(\hat{y},y^{\star})\log\pi(\hat{z},\hat{y}\mid x;\theta)\right]+{}`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\!\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{\hat{z},\hat{y}\sim q(\cdot\mid x,y^{\star};\theta^{(k-1)})}\!\left[r(\hat{y},y^{\star})\left(1-\log q(\hat{z},\hat{y}\mid x,y^{\star};\theta^{(k-1)})\right)\right]}_{\triangleq C}\,,`$ |  |  |

where $`C\geq 0`$ is independent of $`\theta`$. The tightness follows
from the fact that $`z=1+\log z`$ if and only if $`z=1`$. ∎

## Appendix C Ablations Studies

Figure 4: Test accuracy, data utilization, and reasoning length for Qwen
3B and HelpSteer2 helpfulness.

We experiment with various rejection sampling budgets $`M\in\{1,3,5\}`$
in $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt RS`$. In
[Figure 4](#A3.F4 "In Appendix C Ablations Studies ‣ Learning to Reason in LLMs by Expectation Maximization"),
we show an example where the accuracy clearly increases with $`M`$. This
gain is due to increased data utilization. However, even with this
improvement, $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt RS`$ is less accurate than both
$`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPS`$ and $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt STaR`$. In
addition, its computation time is (in the worst-case) linear in $`M`$
and thus $`M`$ times higher than that of $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPS`$.
We summarize the highest accuracies attained by all sampling schemes on
HelpSteer2 dataset in
[Table 3](#A3.T3 "In Appendix C Ablations Studies ‣ Learning to Reason in LLMs by Expectation Maximization").
In all cases, the accuracies of $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPS`$ are higher
than those of any rejection sampling scheme.

| Metric | Base | $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt RS\mathchar 45\relax 1`$ | $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt RS\mathchar 45\relax 3`$ | $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt RS\mathchar 45\relax 5`$ | $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt STaR`$ | $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPS`$ |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Helpfulness | 30.44 | 29.97 | 31.81 | 34.30 | 36.91 | 37.71 |
| Correctness | 28.30 | 26.59 | 27.96 | 27.86 | 40.51 | 43.91 |
| Coherence | 36.75 | 34.28 | 36.00 | 37.56 | 62.73 | 67.55 |
| Complexity | 15.94 | 22.68 | 37.91 | 40.43 | 50.98 | 51.60 |
| Verbosity | 23.09 | 42.82 | 56.16 | 58.37 | 58.99 | 59.04 |

Table 3: Highest test accuracies for Qwen 3B on all metrics in
HelpSteer2 dataset across $`M\in\{1,3,5\}`$ for
$`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt RS`$.

Figure 5: Test accuracy, data utilization, and reasoning length for Qwen
3B and HelpSteer2 coherence.

We further examine robustness to the conditioning prompt. We experiment
with two variants of the hint in
[Figure 1](#S3.F1 "In 3 Rationale Sampling ‣ Learning to Reason in LLMs by Expectation Maximization").
The first is “The score of the response should be {conditioning}. Do not
output the hint.”, and we denote the corresponding algorithms by
$`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPS2`$ and $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt STaR2`$. The
second is “The score of the response should be {conditioning}.”. The
corresponding algorithms are denoted by $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPS3`$
and $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt STaR3`$. We show plots for all prompts and
HelpSteer2 coherence in
[Figure 5](#A3.F5 "In Appendix C Ablations Studies ‣ Learning to Reason in LLMs by Expectation Maximization").
While the absolute accuracy of the new prompts decreases, the relative
ranking of the sampling schemes remains unchanged, confirming that our
findings generalize beyond a single prompt. Crucially, this accuracy
drop highlights that the prompt formulation matters: precise
conditioning that explicitly instructs the LLM *how* to use the evidence
yields better results than simply stating the evidence as a fact. We
summarize the highest accuracies attained by all sampling schemes on
HelpSteer2 dataset in
[Table 4](#A3.T4 "In Appendix C Ablations Studies ‣ Learning to Reason in LLMs by Expectation Maximization").
In all cases, $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPS`$ has higher accuracies than
$`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt STaR`$, $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPS2`$ has
higher accuracies than $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt STaR2`$, and
$`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPS3`$ has higher accuracies than
$`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt STaR3`$.

| Metric | Base | $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt RS`$ | $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt STaR`$ | $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPS`$ | $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt STaR2`$ | $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPS2`$ | $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt STaR3`$ | $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPS3`$ |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|

Finally, we experiment with various dataset sizes
$`N\in\{1\,000,2\,000,4\,000\}`$ in
[Table 5](#A3.T5 "In Appendix C Ablations Studies ‣ Learning to Reason in LLMs by Expectation Maximization").
We observe that when the dataset is much smaller than in our experiment
($`N=1\,000`$), both $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt STaR`$ and
$`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPS`$ perform poorly and there is no major
difference in their accuracies. On the other hand, when the dataset is
much larger ($`N=4\,000`$), both $`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt STaR`$ and
$`\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPS`$ perform comparably to $`N=2\,000`$ and our
earlier reported trends hold.
````
